Harrison ORCID: orcid.org/0000-0001-7215-9393 4 , 5 , 6 & … Daniel Kahne ORCID: orcid.org/0000-0002-8296-1424 1 Show authors Nature ( 2026 ) Cite this article Save article View saved research 30k Accesses 27 Altmetric Metrics details Abstract Gram-negative bacteria are surrounded by a multilayered cell envelope with a mostly impermeable outer membrane that provides intrinsic resistance to many antibiotics 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 . The outer membrane is an asymmetrical bilayer with phospholipids in the inner leaflet and lipopolysaccharide (LPS) in the outer leaflet 6 , 7 . An LPS transport (Lpt) machine called LptB 2 FGCADE moves LPS across a protein bridge from the inner membrane to the outer membrane 8 , 9 . LPS biosynthesis is regulated to prevent toxic accumulation of LPS molecules in the inner membrane during growth 10 , 11 , 12 . Whether LPS transport across the Lpt bridge is also regulated has been unclear. Here we present three structures of the trans-envelope Lpt complex in LPS-free, LPS-bound and ATP-bound states, along with a structure of a partial bridge. These structures, combined with biochemical experiments, show that Lpt bridge assembly triggers movement of the transmembrane helix of LptC (TM-LptC) in an LPS-dependent manner, resulting in increased ATP binding and hydrolysis. We also show that LPS transport in vivo requires bridge formation and movement of the TM-LptC. Our data support a model in which assembled Lpt bridges respond to the presence of LPS in the inner membrane to turn on transport by moving the TM-LptC, thus coordinating LPS transport activity with bridge assembly and the presence of LPS at the inner membrane. Cryoelectron microscopy Lipopolysaccharides Membrane proteins Regulation of Carbon Metabolism in Pseudomonas Species Main Bacterial cells have an inner (cytoplasmic) membrane (IM) containing protein machines that assemble other cell-envelope layers, such as the peptidoglycan cell wall. Gram-negative bacteria also have an outer membrane (OM) that surrounds the peptidoglycan cell wall 1 , 2 . This OM has a phospholipid inner leaflet and an LPS outer leaflet 6 , 7 . The LPS layer of the OM excludes many antibiotics that are effective against Gram-positive bacteria, greatly limiting therapeutic strategies to treat Gram-negative infections 4 , 5 . LPS is synthesized at the IM and must be transported across the aqueous periplasm and through the OM to the cell surface 3 . The LPS transport (Lpt) machinery consists of an IM ABC transporter complex (LptB 2 FGC), an OM translocon (LptDE) and a soluble periplasmic protein (LptA) 13 , 14 , 15 , 16 , 17 , 18 , 19 , 20 , 21 (Fig. 1a ). During the transport of LPS to the cell surface, LptA assembles with the two membrane complexes, forming a continuous trans-envelope protein bridge (LptB 2 FGCADE) 22 . LptB 2 FGCADE uses the energy from ATP binding and hydrolysis in the cytoplasm to extract LPS from the IM and transport it against its concentration gradient directly to the outer leaflet of the OM 22 , 23 , 24 , 25 , 26 , 27 . Fig. 1: Structure of the trans-envelope Lpt protein bridge bound to LPS. Full size image a , Cartoon schematic showing the LPS transport proteins in the unassembled (left) and assembled (right) states. LPS is transported across a membrane-spanning protein bridge. P i , inorganic phosphate. b , Representative electron micrograph of LptB 2 FGCADE complexes purified in detergent. Dotted white circles indicate selected LptB 2 FGCADE complexes. The representative micrograph was chosen to contain approximately the median number of particles per micrograph out of particles included in the final reconstruction. Scale bar, 50 nm. c , Representative 2D class averages generated in cryoSPARC, with orientation aligned to aid visualization. Scale bar, 210 Å. d , Composite density for LPS-bound LptB 2 FGCADE consisting of the local refinements of LptADE and LptB 2 FGC, shown from a front view perpendicular to the micelle containing LptDE. The consensus map used for local refinement, low-pass filtered to 10 Å, is shown as a transparent envelope. Cross-sections of the LptB 2 FGCADE density at the indicated positions are shown. For comparisons of the IM and OM refinements of LptB 2 FGCADE with previously reported structures of Lpt subcomplexes 38 , 57 , 60 , 61 , see Supplementary Fig. 5 . e , Model of LptB 2 FGCADE shown in the same view and colours as in d . The periplasmic domains of LptFG did not refine to high resolution; for visualization, these regions of LptF (residues 137–246) and LptG (residues 142–244) from Protein Data Bank (PDB) 6MHU were fitted as rigid bodies into the consensus structure and are shown in semi-transparent grey. The dotted box indicates the position of the magnified views shown in f . f , Magnified views of the periplasmic portion of the bridge viewed from different angles to illustrate the opening that accommodates the LPS substrate during transport. A key requirement for LPS transport is that newly synthesized LPS must be transported to the OM efficiently to prevent toxic build-up of LPS at the IM. One mechanism of controlling cellular LPS levels is to turn off LPS biosynthesis 10 , 11 . Regulation of the rate of LPS transport would provide an alternative strategy to control IM LPS levels, but it has been unclear whether such regulation occurs. The rate of LPS transport depends on how many bridges exist and whether they are in an active state. Two types of LptB 2 FGCADE bridge with different lifetimes have been observed in cells, and we have proposed that only the longer-lived bridges actively transport LPS 28 . Reducing the levels of LPS decreases the fraction of Lpt components that form assembled bridges in cells, which implies that bridge assembly depends on LPS 28 . However, the mechanism that underlies the formation of active bridges has been unclear. Here we present three distinct structures of the assembled Lpt bridge, together with a structure of a partial bridge. These structures, combined with biochemistry, reveal the molecular mechanisms that control the formation of active Lpt bridges. Stabilization of assembled Lpt bridges To obtain a structure of the full Lpt bridge, we first attempted to isolate intact bridges directly from cells, but the assembled bridges dissociated during purification (Supplementary Fig. 1 ). We therefore sought to reconstitute the bridge in vitro from separately purified subcomplexes. We have previously shown that a variant of the IM subcomplex in which LptA is fused to LptC as a single polypeptide joined by a flexible poly-glycine-serine linker (hereafter termed LptC–LptA fusion) is able to form Lpt bridges 28 . Bridges formed with the IM subcomplex containing the LptC–LptA fusion (hereafter termed LptB 2 FGCA) are more stable in cells than are wild-type bridges, so allowed us to avoid the tendency of soluble LptA to oligomerize when assembling Lpt bridges in vitro 18 , 28 , 29 (Extended Data Fig. 1a ). We confirmed that the LptC–LptA fusion allows growth on minimal medium in the absence of native LptC and LptA (Extended Data Fig. 1b–d ) and assessed the activity of LptB 2 FGCA through in vivo and in vitro assays. We observe in vivo site-specific cross-linking of the LptC–LptA fusion to LPS at positions known to cross-link LPS in the individual proteins (Extended Data Fig. 1e ). The ATPase activity of LptB 2 FGCA in proteoliposomes is similar to that of LptB 2 FGC (Extended Data Fig. 1f ) and we used a flow-cytometry-based assay to confirm that LptB 2 FGCA can form bridges with LptDE in vitro without the addition of soluble LptA (refs. 22 , 30 ; Extended Data Fig. 1g and Supplementary Fig. 2 ). Thus, LptB 2 FGCA recapitulates the functions of the individual LptC and LptA proteins both in vivo and in biochemical assays. We also stabilized the interface between LptD and LptA by site-specifically incorporating the photocrosslinkable amino acid p -benzoyl- l -phenylalanine ( p BPA) at position Y63 in the N-terminal domain of LptD. This site has been shown to cross-link to LptA with high efficiency 31 . We separately purified LptB 2 FGCA and LptD(Y63 p BPA)E in detergent and co-incubated the purified complexes while exposing to ultraviolet (UV) light. We detected high-efficiency cross-link formation, enabling purification of the full bridge by size-exclusion chromatography (SEC) (Supplementary Fig. 3 ). We prepared samples for cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) using the purified, covalently stabilized bridge (LptB 2 FGCAD(Y63 p BPA)E; hereafter, LptB 2 FGCADE). We observed dumbbell-shaped particles, consistent with two connected membrane complexes (Fig. 1b and Extended Data Fig. 2 ). The two-dimensional (2D) class averages showed that the angle between the IM protein complex and the bridge is variable (Fig. 1c ), indicating a high degree of flexibility in this region. The flexibility limited our ability to simultaneously resolve the IM and OM portions of the Lpt bridge to high resolution. We therefore performed local refinements focused on the region of the structure comprising either LptB 2 FGC or LptADE starting from a consensus map of the LptB 2 FGCADE bridge (Extended Data Fig. 2 ). These refinements yielded a 3.3-Å-resolution density map for the IM portion and a 3.4-Å-resolution density map for the OM region of LptB 2 FGCADE. We integrated these local refinements into the consensus map to construct a composite density map (Fig. 1d ) for the Lpt bridge and built a model corresponding to this composite map (Fig. 1e ). The periplasmic domains of LptFG (LptF residues 137–246; LptG residues 142–244) remained poorly resolved in the composite map because of flexible connections to their respective TM regions and were therefore not modelled. We speculate that the observed flexibility of the LptFG periplasmic domains in bridges could be required to allow the formation of a trans-envelope complex (results of three-dimensional (3D) variability analysis are shown in Supplementary Fig. 4 and Supplementary Video 1 ). Proteins in the OM are mostly immobile, whereas IM proteins can laterally diffuse freely 32 , 33 . Thus, the flexibility we observe could afford LptB 2 FGC a range of 2D motion in the IM to move relative to LptDE without breaking the bridge. Structure of the LptB 2 FGCADE bridge The Lpt trans-envelope complex is an elongated structure, approximately 280 Å in length from edge to edge of the membrane complexes (Fig. 1d ). There is clear density corresponding to a LPS molecule bound in the lumen formed by the TM helices of LptFG (hereafter, LptFG lumen; Fig. 1d , panels 7 and 8). The periplasmic domain is approximately 150 Å in length, somewhat shorter than the estimated periplasmic dimension for Escherichia coli 34 (180–240 Å). It is possible that Lpt bridges in vivo incorporate more than one copy of LptA (approximately 40 Å), although our data indicate that the LptC–LptA fusion with no free LptA is viable (Extended Data Fig. 1b–d ). The structure shows that the IM and OM complexes are connected by the β-jellyroll domains of LptF, LptC, LptA and LptD, which assemble to form a groove that spirals slightly 8 , 18 , 35 , 36 (Fig. 1f ). We propose that the spiralling groove serves to minimize clashes between the oligosaccharide portions of adjacent LPS molecules as they are being trafficked. Cross-sections perpendicular to the long axis of the groove show variability in the space available to accommodate the LPS substrate (Fig. 1d , panels 1–6). A representation of the internal volume of the periplasm chute calculated with pyKVFinder 37 is shown in Extended Data Fig. 3 . The concave surface of the groove is lined predominantly with hydrophobic residues, consistent with the idea that this groove accommodates the acyl chains of LPS during transit to the OM. However, we observe some constriction points in the chute, with insufficient volume to allow passage of LPS. Thus, conformational flexibility in the periplasmic domains must be required to allow LPS transport. The TM helices of LptF and LptG and the bound LPS molecule are well resolved in our local refinement of the LptB 2 FGC portion of the Lpt bridge, but we did not detect density for the TM helix of LptC (TM-LptC), which suggests that the TM-LptC is not ordered in our structure of the Lpt bridge bound to LPS (Fig. 1d,e ). Moreover, the TM helices of LptFG adopt a conformation more similar to that seen for LptB 2 FG (root mean square deviation (RMSD) < 1 Å) than to that of LptB 2 FGC (RMSD = 2.3 Å) (refs. 32 , 33 , 34 , 35 ; Supplementary Fig. 5 ). In this conformation, the helices of LptFG make close contacts with the bound LPS molecule. Previous structural work has shown that the TM-LptC is not resolved when LptB in the LptB 2 FGC complex is bound to nucleotide in the closed dimer conformation 38 , 39 . However, it has been unclear whether the TM-LptC moves because ATP binds and promotes LptB dimerization or whether movement of the TM-LptC allows ATP binding 38 , 39 , 40 , 41 . Our structure of LptB 2 FGCADE suggests that in the context of the assembled Lpt bridge, the TM-LptC can move before nucleotide binding. Structure of the Lpt bridge not bound to LPS We wondered if it would be possible to obtain a structure with LPS on the periplasmic portion of the Lpt bridge rather than in the LptFG lumen. We have previously established that residue T47 in LptC, when substituted with p BPA, forms a very strong cross-link to LPS 23 , 30 . We have proposed that LPS binds in this location after extraction from the IM. We site-specifically incorporated p BPA at T47 in the LptC–LptA fusion and attempted to obtain structures with LPS trapped on the bridge by purifying LptB 2 FGC(T47 p BPA)A from cells exposed to UV light before protein purification. We detected LPS cross-linking to LptB 2 FGC(T47 p BPA)A by immunoblotting and used this LPS-cross-linked complex to prepare bridges (hereafter, LptB 2 FGC(T47 p BPA)ADE; Extended Data Fig. 4 ). We solved the cryo-EM structure using a similar approach to that used for the structure above (Fig. 2a,b and Extended Data Fig. 4 ). We again observed considerable flexibility between the periplasmic and TM domains of LptFG, which resulted in these regions being unresolved in our density maps (Supplementary Fig. 4 and Supplementary Video 1 ). Because this unresolved region includes LptC T47, we were unable to visualize the cross-linked LPS. Fig. 2: Dissociation of the TM-LptC requires LPS binding and Lpt bridge formation. The periplasmic domains of LptFGC and LptA, which did not refine to high resolution, were modelled as rigid fits of domains from PDB 6MHU or the LPS-free LptB 2 FGCADE and are shown in transparent grey. e , Representative immunoblots showing the uncrosslinked LPS present in each sample used for structure determination, with anti-LptB used as a loading control. Blots with different antibodies represent identical samples processed in parallel. f , IM local refinement of LptB 2 FGCADE bound to LPS. Bottom, top view of the model for the LPS-bound lumenal region of LptB 2 FGCADE. g , IM local refinement of LPS-free LptB 2 FGCADE. Bottom, top view of the model for the LPS-free lumenal region of LptB 2 FGCADE. h , LptB 2 FGCA bound to LPS. Top, density for LPS-bound LptB 2 FGCA, low-pass-filtered to 4.1 Å, with views as in f . Bottom, top view of the model for the LPS-bound lumenal region of LptB 2 FGCA. The OM portions of the two bridges are very similar (RMSD < 0.5 Å); however, the IM local refinement of LptB 2 FGC(T47 p BPA)ADE has well-resolved density for the TM-LptC and adopts a conformation similar to that of LptB 2 FGC (Supplementary Fig. 6 ). Moreover, there was no clear density for LPS in the LptFG lumen for the LptB 2 FGC(T47 p BPA)ADE bridge (Fig. 2g ). We compared the relative amount of LPS that copurified with each of the two Lpt bridge preparations (Fig. 2e , lanes 1 and 2) and found that the LptB 2 FGC(T47 p BPA)ADE sample contained a small amount of uncrosslinked LPS relative to the LptB 2 FGCADE sample. We also obtained a low-resolution structure of LptB 2 FGCADE lacking LPS in the LptFG lumen (Extended Data Fig. 5 ), and the TM-LptC in this structure is ordered. Thus, when there is no LPS in the LptFG lumen, the TM-LptC is in its resting position even in the intact bridge. Together, the two types of bridge structure—that is, with and without LPS bound in the LptFG lumen—suggest that LPS binding causes a conformational change in the TM helices of LptFG with concomitant delocalization of the TM-LptC. We refer to these two states of the Lpt bridges as the LPS-bound or the LPS-free state on the basis of whether the LptFG lumen contains LPS. The TM-LptC moves when bridges form with LPS Our two structures of the Lpt bridge imply that LPS binding in the LptFG lumen and dissociation of the TM-LptC are linked. However, previous structures of LptB 2 FGC with LPS bound in the LptFG lumen show that the TM-LptC is ordered 38 , 39 . Hence, we wondered whether movement of the TM-LptC is dependent not only on LPS, but also on bridge formation. We prepared a sample of LPS-bound LptB 2 FGCA (Fig. 2e , lane 3) and determined its structure by cryo-EM to a resolution of 3.1 Å (Fig. 2c,d , Extended Data Fig. 6 and Supplementary Video 2 ). We detected clear density in the LptFG lumen for both LPS and the ordered TM-LptC (Fig. 2h ). By contrast, in the LPS-bound and LPS-free structures of LptB 2 FGCADE, we observed either clearly resolved density for LPS in the LptFG lumen but no density for the TM-LptC (LPS-bound LptB 2 FGCADE; Fig. 2f ) or well-resolved density for the TM-LptC and negligible density for LPS in the LptFG lumen (LPS-free bridges; Fig. 2g ). To compare the conformations of the IM portions of each structure, we aligned the models for each structure based on LptF (Fig. 2f–h , bottom panels). The position of LPS is similar in LPS-bound LptB 2 FGCA and the LPS-bound full bridge; however, the TM helices of LptG shift from the more open state observed in the LPS-bound LptB 2 FGCA and the LPS-free full bridge to a more constricted state in the LPS-bound full bridge. The shift in the positions of TM helices 1–3 of LptG, which allows the formation of stabilizing interactions with the bound LPS, displaces the TM-LptC. This conformational change occurs only in the context of the full Lpt bridge (see Supplementary Fig. 7 for additional comparisons to published structures 38 ). Because LptB 2 FGCADE is formed from purified Lpt subcomplexes without nucleotide added, we conclude that the TM-LptC can move independent of nucleotide binding only in the assembled, LPS-loaded Lpt bridge. The TM-LptC regulates ATP binding affinity Previous work has shown that the TM-LptC regulates the ATP hydrolysis activity of IM Lpt complexes 30 , 38 . We tested the LPS transport activity of IM complexes with and without the TM-LptC at different ATP concentrations using our established biochemical transport assay that monitors LPS transport to LptA by site-specific photocrosslinking 23 (Extended Data Fig. 7a ). In this assay, p BPA is incorporated at position I36 in LptA and LPS cross-linking to LptA is monitored over time for IM complexes in proteoliposomes containing LPS, incubated in the presence of ATP and LptA. We found that LptB 2 FG(ΔTM-LptC) was able to transport LPS to LptA at lower concentrations of ATP, compared with complexes containing full-length LptC. This result suggests that IM complexes lacking the TM-LptC have a higher affinity for ATP than do wild-type IM complexes, consistent with previous findings that ΔTM-LptC suppresses defects of LptB variants that are deficient in ATP binding 40 . We measured the ATP binding affinity for catalytically inactive (containing an LptB E163Q mutation) LptB(E163Q) 2 FG and LptB(E163Q) 2 FGC in the presence and absence of LPS using a scintillation proximity assay (SPA; Fig. 3a and Supplementary Figs. 8 and 9 ). LptB(E163Q) 2 FG binds more tightly to ATP (equilibrium dissociation constant ( K d ) ≈ 20 μM) than does LptB(E163Q) 2 FGC ( K d ≈ 40 μM). In both cases, the measured binding affinities were unchanged by the presence of LPS. We also measured the ATP binding affinity for the partial bridge (LptB(E163Q) 2 FGCA) and the full bridge (LptB(E163Q) 2 FGCADE) in the presence and absence of LPS. We found that the ATP binding affinity of the partial bridge with or without LPS resembled that of LptB(E163Q) 2 FGC (Fig. 3b ). For the full bridge, however, there was a difference in ATP binding affinity with and without LPS. In the presence of LPS, the ATP binding affinity matched that of LptB(E163Q) 2 FG ( K d ≈ 20 μM), whereas in the absence of LPS, the ATP binding affinity matched that of LptB(E163Q) 2 FGC ( K d ≈ 40 μM; Fig. 3b ). A table summarizing the K d values is shown in Fig. 3e . These results suggest that the presence of LPS in full Lpt bridges changes the ATP binding affinity by displacing the TM-LptC from its binding site. Fig. 3: LPS-bound Lpt bridges have higher ATP affinity and ATPase activity.
