Catalytically dead LptB(E163Q) was used to prevent ATP turnover. Data are mean ± s.d. from three independent experiments. b , Equilibrium binding affinity of ATP to LptB(E163Q) 2 FGCA and LptB(E163Q) 2 FGCADE measured in the presence or absence of added LPS by SPA. Catalytically dead LptB(E163Q) was used to prevent ATP turnover. Data are mean ± s.d. from three independent experiments. c , Composite density map of ATP-bound LptB(E163Q) 2 FGCADE consisting of the local refinements of LptADE and LptB(E163Q) 2 FGC, shown from a front view perpendicular to the micelle containing LptDE. The consensus map used for local refinement, low-pass-filtered to 10 Å, is shown as a transparent outline. d , Semi-transparent density map for the IM-focused local refinement of ATP-bound LptB(E163Q) 2 FGCADE, shown from front and top views with PDB 6MI8 (a model corresponding to vanadate-bound LptB 2 FGC) docked. e , Table summarizing the K d values for the experiments presented in a , b . The mean of three independent experiments was analysed by a cooperative binding model yielding K d . f , ATPase activity of LptB 2 FGCA in proteoliposomes without or with LPS, measured with increasing amounts of proteoliposomes containing LptDE added to the reactions. Experiments were performed in duplicate. The LptDE-alone sample contained an equivalent molar amount of LptDE in proteoliposomes to that of the sample with a 64-fold molar ratio of LptDE to LptB 2 FGCA. g , ATPase activity of LptB 2 FGCA in proteoliposomes without or with LPS, incubated with or without a 56-fold molar ratio of LptDE in proteoliposomes. Data are mean ± s.d. from three independent experiments. Source data Structure of Lpt bridge bound to ATP To assess whether ATP binding to the catalytically dead LptB(E163Q) 2 FGCADE bridges leads to LptB dimerization and collapse of the LptFG lumen, we obtained a structure of the LptB(E163Q) 2 FGCADE bridge bound to ATP. We purified catalytically inactive LptB(E163Q) 2 FGCADE bridges following the same procedure we used to purify the LPS-bound LptB 2 FGCADE bridges and incubated them with ATP and MgCl 2 before sample preparation for cryo-EM. Following a similar data-processing workflow to that used for the other full Lpt bridge datasets, we obtained an OM local refinement that resolved to 4.5 Å; however, heterogeneity of the IM region prevented us from obtaining a high-resolution local refinement for the same particle set (Extended Data Fig. 8 ). After 3D classification, we obtained a local refinement of the IM complex bound to ATP that resolved to 7.4 Å. The corresponding OM local refinement for the same particle subset resolved to 7.0 Å, and we constructed a composite map from these local refinements (Fig. 3c and Extended Data Fig. 8 ). At this resolution, α-helices are clearly resolved and the structure of the IM complex for this particle subset is in close agreement with previously determined structures of LptB 2 FGC bound to nucleotide 38 (Fig. 3d ). In this conformation, LptB is in a closed dimer, the TM helices of LptFG have rearranged to constrict the LptFG lumen and there is no resolved density for the TM-LptC. Thus, assembled Lpt bridges pass through the same nucleotide-bound intermediate state in the catalytic cycle as partial bridges do. We propose that the differences in ATP binding we observe for Lpt bridges with and without LPS reflect whether ATP binding is required to facilitate TM-LptC movement or not. We observed one additional class for the IM portion of ATP-bound LptB(E163Q) 2 FGCADE; this resolved to 9.2 Å and exhibited ordered density for only one copy of LptB, which is bound to LptF (Extended Data Fig. 8 ). Previous data have suggested 42 that LptB interacts differently with LptF than it does with LptG; however, understanding the relevance of the low-resolution subpopulation we observe will require further experiments. Highest ATPase activity for LPS-bound Lpt bridge A puzzling aspect of Lpt machine function has been that LptB 2 FGC, unlike typical ABC transporters, does not show an activation of ATPase activity in response to the presence of its substrate 43 . However, differences in ATPase activity have been observed between LptB 2 FG, LptB 2 FGC and LptB 2 FGC(ΔTM), with the presence of the TM-LptC resulting in decreased ATPase activity 30 , 38 . We tested the ATPase activity of proteoliposomes containing LptB 2 FGCA with and without LPS and incubated with increasing amounts of proteoliposomes containing LptDE. For samples that did not contain LPS, ATPase activity was similar regardless of the mole fraction of LptDE proteoliposomes (Fig. 3f ). However, ATPase activity increased markedly as LptDE was added to LptB 2 FGCA proteoliposomes containing LPS (Fig. 3f ). Compared with LptB 2 FGCA alone, the ATPase activity increased considerably when both LPS and a high mole fraction of LptDE were present (Fig. 3g ). This increase in ATPase activity for Lpt bridges bound to LPS shows that activity turns on in response to the presence of substrate, but only when trans-envelope Lpt bridges are assembled. TM-LptC moves to transport LPS in vivo To test the relationship between Lpt bridge assembly and TM-LptC localization in vivo, we introduced a change in LptA (LptA(A152R)) that prevents association with LptD and formation of trans-envelope Lpt complexes (Fig. 4a ). A similar change in LptC (LptC(G153R)) disrupts association with LptA (refs. 35 , 44 ; Extended Data Fig. 7b ). To test whether Lpt bridge formation affects the localization of the TM-LptC in vivo, we overexpressed either wild-type LptB 2 FGCA or LptB 2 FGCA(A152R) with p BPA incorporated at position I33 in TM1 of LptG, which is located in close proximity to the TM-LptC (Fig. 4b , top). We detected increased cross-link formation between LptG and LptC for the mutant that prevents the assembly of Lpt bridges, suggesting that dissociation of the TM-LptC depends on bridge assembly in vivo (Fig. 4b , bottom). Fig. 4: Dissociation of the TM-LptC in vivo depends on bridge assembly and is required for LPS transport. Full size image a , Top, close-up view of LPS-free LptB 2 FGCADE showing the interface between LptA (red) and LptD (blue), with the position of A152R indicated in yellow. Bottom, immunoblots detecting bridge components from copurifications of wild-type (WT) LptCA and LptCA(A152R) (eluate), with inputs shown on the left. b , Top, close-up view of LPS-free LptB 2 FGCA showing the position of LptG(I33 p BPA) (yellow star). Bottom, LptB 2 FGCA and LptB 2 FGCA(A152R) complexes were subjected to UV cross-linking in vivo and adducts were detected by immunoblotting for LptG. LptG cross-links to LptCA only when bridges cannot form. c , Photocrosslinking experiments were performed in vivo for LptB 2 FGCA and LptB 2 FGCA(A152R) with or without the TM-LptC. p BPA was incorporated at LptA L116 in the LptCA fusion. LPS and LptCA were detected by immunoblotting with anti-LPS and anti-His antibodies. Dissociation of the TM-LptC is required for LPS transport to LptA in vivo. d , Serial dilutions of E. coli strains expressing wild-type LptE or LptE(K136D) and with or without the TM-LptC were spotted on MacConkey agar at the indicated dilutions. e , The LptE K136D mutation does not prevent the formation of Lpt bridges. Formation of LptB 2 FGCADE complexes was assessed by pulling down His-tagged wild-type LptB 2 FGCA in a background of wild-type or mutant LptE and immunoblotting with antibodies against LptD, LptE and LptC–His. f , The LptE K136D mutation increases cross-link formation between the TM-LptC and LptG. LptB 2 FGCA with p BPA at LptG I33 was expressed in a background of wild-type or mutant LptE and photocrosslinked in vivo. Adducts were detected by blotting for LptC–His. g , Deleting the TM-LptC restores LPS transport in a LptE(K136D) background. LptB 2 FGC and LptB 2 FGC(ΔTM) were expressed with LptA(L116 p BPA) in a background of either wild-type LptE or LptE(K136D) and photocrosslinked in vivo. Cross-linking was detected by immunoblotting for LPS and LptC–His. All data are representative of three independent experiments. Blots against different antibodies represent identical samples processed in parallel. To test the effect of bridge assembly and TM-LptC delocalization on LPS transport in vivo, we incorporated p BPA at position L116 in LptA and assayed cross-linking of LPS at this position for wild-type and LptA(A152R) complexes with and without the TM-LptC. For the wild-type complexes that are competent for bridge formation, we observed similar levels of LPS cross-linking in the presence and absence of the TM-LptC (Fig. 4c ). However, when bridge formation was prevented, we observed cross-links to LPS only when the TM-LptC was absent, indicating that delocalization of the TM-LptC is required for LPS transport to occur in vivo (Fig. 4c ). We obtained similar results using the LptC(G153R) mutant and assaying LPS transport by monitoring cross-linking to LptC(T47) (Extended Data Fig. 7c,d ). Together, our results suggest that the TM-LptC has an important role in regulating LPS transport. Although the TM-LptC is not strictly essential, the fact that full-length LptC is broadly conserved implies a strong selection for the retention of the TM-LptC (refs. 35 , 40 , 45 ). LptC(ΔTM) rescues OM translocon defects Because the LPS transporter increases activity in response to LPS bound in the TM cavity of the LptB 2 FGC complex in assembled bridges, we wondered whether the TM-LptC can also respond to the build-up of LPS at the OM translocon LptDE to turn off transport once the outer leaflet is full. We have previously shown that a variant of LptE, LptE(K136D), has reduced binding affinity for LPS, resulting in OM permeability 46 . Furthermore, in vitro LPS transport assays have shown that less LPS is transported by LptDE complexes containing LptE(K136D) and that ATP hydrolysis for such transport also decreases 25 , 47 . To test the role of the TM-LptC in the LPS transport defects observed for LptE(K136D), we tested the growth of LptE(K136D), LptC(ΔTM) double-mutant bacteria and found that growth on MacConkey agar was restored for the LptE(K136D) variant when the TM-LptC was deleted (Fig. 4d ). To characterize the mechanistic basis of the growth rescue, we characterized bridge assembly and localization of the TM-LptC in the LptE(K136D) background. We found that LptE(K136D) does not prevent the assembly of Lpt bridges, but that cross-linking of the TM-LptC to LptG increases, implying increased TM-LptC localization proximal to LptG (Fig. 4e,f ). Consistent with these results, we found that LPS cross-linking to LptA in the LptE(K136D) background with full-length LptC is decreased and that deletion of the TM-LptC restores LPS transport, explaining the growth rescue and suggesting that the TM-LptC also modulates transport activity in response to changes at the OM translocon (Fig. 4g ). The bridge binds to multiple LPS molecules We have previously proposed a ‘PEZ’ model for LPS transport, in which each LPS molecule extracted from the IM by LptB 2 FGC pushes the previous LPS along the length of the Lpt bridge to the OM, similar to a PEZ sweet dispenser 8 , 23 . As we were unable to structurally characterize the Lpt bridge with LPS bound in the periplasmic region (see above), we sought biochemical support for the PEZ model of transport. The PEZ model suggests that it should be possible to capture simultaneous LPS cross-linking at multiple positions in the bridge. We therefore incorporated p BPA at sites in LptC and LptA in the same Lpt complex (LptB 2 FGC(T47 p BPA)A(L116 p BPA)) and assessed LPS cross-linking in vitro in the presence of excess LPS to maximize the chances of capturing a double cross-link. We used a variant of the LptCA fusion with a thrombin cleavage site incorporated into the linker to allow detection of the number of LPS molecules cross-linked to LptCA (uncleaved) and analysis of the relative ratios of LPS cross-linking to LptC versus LptA (after thrombin cleavage; Fig. 5a ). We observed two LPS-reactive bands corresponding to LptCA cross-linked to one or two LPS molecules before thrombin cleavage, and bands corresponding to LPS cross-linked to either LptC or LptA after thrombin cleavage (Fig. 5b ). Analysis of the cross-linking to LptC and LptA after thrombin cleavage shows that cross-links accumulate at LptC and LptA at approximately equal ratios over time, as would be predicted by the PEZ model. In fact, we could also observe multiple LPS cross-links to LptB 2 FGC(T47 p BPA)A(L116 p BPA) in vivo (Fig. 5c ). This supports the hypothesis that in vivo LPS transport occurs by the PEZ model, which would allow the transport of more LPS per unit time. Fig. 5: Detection of multiple, simultaneous LPS cross-links both in vitro and in vivo provides support for the PEZ model. Full size image a , Schematic for the detection of multiple LPS cross-links. LptB 2 FGCA complexes were substituted at LptC T47 and LptA L116 with p BPA (orange stars). A thrombin cleavage site (grey) added in the linker between LptC and LptA allows analysis of cross-linking to individual proteins after digestion of the linker. b , Simultaneous in vitro photocrosslinking of LPS to LptC and LptA. Purified LptB 2 FGC(T47 p BPA)A(L116 p BPA) was incubated with LPS, and transport was initiated by adding ATP. Samples were removed at the indicated time points and exposed to UV light, and cross-linking was analysed before and after thrombin cleavage by western blotting with an anti-LPS antibody using anti-His and anti-LptC as loading controls. CA, LptC(T47 p BPA)A(L116 p BPA) fusion before thrombin cleavage; A, cLptA(L116pBPA) after thrombin cleavage; C, LptC(T47 p BPA) after thrombin cleavage. c , Simultaneous in vivo photocrosslinking of LPS to LptC and LptA. Proteins substituted at both LptC T47 and LptA L116 with p BPA were overexpressed in E. coli . Samples were taken during mid-log phase and exposed to UV light, and cross-linking was analysed both before and after thrombin cleavage by western blotting with an anti-LPS antibody. All western blot data are representative of three independent experiments performed with similar results. Blots against different antibodies represent identical samples processed in parallel. Discussion OM biogenesis requires the movement of millions of LPS molecules to the cell surface each division cycle 48 . Transport of LPS to the outer leaflet of the OM through an ATP-powered trans-envelope protein bridge is essential to meet the high demand for efficient trafficking. However, bridge assembly must be coordinated to ensure that LPS does not accumulate in the outer leaflet of the IM or the inner leaflet of the OM, because mislocalization of LPS is toxic 49 , 50 . Previous studies have shown that the TM-LptC must move to allow the ATP-dependent dimerization of LptB monomers, which is necessary for LPS transport 38 , 39 , 40 , 41 . We have now shown that dissociation of the TM-LptC occurs when assembled Lpt bridges are bound to LPS. In this ‘primed’ state (Fig. 6 ), the TM helices of LptFG, particularly TM1–TM3 of LptG, constrict to maximize contacts with LPS, displacing the TM-LptC and leading to increased ATP binding affinity and ATP hydrolysis activity. Movement of the TM-LptC is required for LPS transport to occur in vivo and provides a link between Lpt transport activity and the presence of LPS in the IM. Furthermore, we show that movement of the TM-LptC mediates changes in transport activity in response to the LptE(K136D) mutation in the OM portion of the transporter, which has lower affinity for LPS. Bridges containing this mutation cannot efficiently insert LPS into the outer leaflet, and transport less LPS because the TM-LptC does not remain in the primed (stably dissociated) state. Previous experiments have shown that reducing the levels of LPS in vivo reduces the fraction of Lpt bridges in a cell 28 . We propose a model in which the LPS transporter responds to the presence of LPS at either the IM or the OM, turning transport up or down by moving the TM-LptC. Fig. 6: Model for LPS transport. Full size image Model for the mechanism of regulation of membrane-to-membrane LPS transport. Coupling Lpt bridge assembly and activity to the presence of LPS in the IM provides a mechanism to increase LPS transport and thus prevent the accumulation of LPS in the IM. In E. coli , there is another mechanism to deal with high concentrations of LPS at the IM that involves degradation of LpxC, the rate-limiting enzyme in the LPS biosynthesis pathway, by the YejM–FtsH protease pair 10 , 12 , 51 , 52 . This mechanism ensures that toxic levels of LPS do not accumulate, but it does so by inhibiting LPS biosynthesis, representing an emergency negative-feedback mechanism. The regulation we describe allows modulation of LPS transport activity in response to LPS levels at the IM and OM and represents a homeostatic mechanism to match the transport of LPS to its cellular abundance. Two other non-essential proteins in the Lpt pathway have recently been identified (LptY and LptM; formerly known as YedD and YifL, respectively) 53 , 54 , 55 , 56 , 57 . Whether these proteins also have a role in modulating flux through the Lpt transport pathway remains to be seen. Our model for the mechanism of LPS transport, informed by the structures of the Lpt bridge and our biochemical experiments, both explains how LPS transport is regulated by the transport machinery, and also changes our understanding of the predominant conformational state of the transporter during active transport in vivo. We now know that during active LPS transport, the TM-LptC is predominantly delocalized, with LPS bound in the TM cavity of LptFG. The LPS transport machinery has attracted considerable attention as a target for therapeutics to treat antibiotic-resistant Gram-negative infections 9 . One compound that targets the Lpt machinery is zosurabalpin 58 , 59 (currently in phase III clinical development), which binds to LPS in LptB 2 FG. Its binding site overlaps with the position of the TM-LptC when it is localized, suggesting that zosurabalpin specifically targets the state of the Lpt transporter with the TM-LptC dissociated; that is, the active state of the Lpt bridge. That zosurabalpin binds to and inhibits the active state of the Lpt transporter helps explain its efficacy. The structures reported here provide a roadmap to understanding how the Lpt bridge regulates LPS transport, and how to design inhibitors of this process. Methods Statistics and reproducibility No statistical methods were used to predetermine sample size. Experiments were not randomized, and investigators were not blinded to allocation during experiments and outcome assessment. For development and verification of Δ lptC , Δ lptA and Δ lptC Δ lptA strains complemented with the LptC–LptA fusion protein (carried on the plasmid pBAD18-LptCA-His), four independent isolates of each strain were phenotypically characterized. After confirming that all selected isolates behaved the same phenotypically, one of them was kept after confirming by PCR (Extended Data Fig. 1b ) that it had the expected chromosomal alleles. All ATP hydrolysis measurements (Fig. 3f,g and Extended Data Fig. 1f ) were made as three independent measurements unless otherwise indicated in the figure legend; data are reported as mean ± s.d. ATP binding measurements (Fig. 3a,b,e ) were made as three independent measurements; data are reported as mean ± s.d. Source data files are provided for all ATP hydrolysis and ATP binding measurements. All western blot data shown are representative of at least three independent replicates that produced similar results (Figs. 2e , 4a–c,e–g and 5b,c and Extended Data Figs. 1d,e and 7a–d ). Representative electron micrographs (Fig. 1b and Extended Data Figs. 2c , 4c , 5c , 6c and 8c ) were chosen to contain approximately the median number of particles per micrograph out of particles included in the final reconstruction for each dataset. The total number of micrographs in each dataset is listed in Extended Data Tables 1 and 2 . All Coomassie gels of the final purified protein samples used for structural characterization (Extended Data Figs. 2b , 4b , 5b , 6b and 8b ) were performed twice. Plasmids, strains and oligonucleotides The strains used in this study are listed in Supplementary Table 1 . All plasmids are listed in Supplementary Table 2 . Plasmids were prepared using Gibson assembly (New England Biolabs) or by site-directed mutagenesis of existing plasmids. All oligonucleotides were purchased from Eton Biosciences, GENEWIZ or Integrated DNA Technologies, and are listed in Supplementary Table 3 . Preparation of lipid and LPS stock solutions To prepare a lipid stock solution, E. coli polar lipid extract (Avanti Polar Lipids) was dissolved in water and sonicated for 30 min to make a 30 mg ml −1 aqueous suspension stock. The lipid stock was flash-frozen in liquid nitrogen and stored at −80 °C. To prepare a 2 mg ml −1 aqueous suspension of LPS, purified LPS extracted from E. coli EH100 (Ra mutant; Sigma) was dissolved in water and sonicated for 30 min. The LPS stock solution was flash-frozen in liquid nitrogen and stored in aliquots at −80 °C. To prepare the fluorescent lipid stock solutions for flow cytometry, E. coli polar lipid extract (Avanti Polar Lipids) was dissolved in chloroform with 1% (molar ratio) ATTO-488 DPPE, ATTO-565 DPPE or ATTO-647N DPPE (ATTO-TEC). Lipid mixtures were dried into a film, hydrated and lyophilized overnight. The lipid mixtures were dissolved in water and sonicated for 30 min to make a 30 mg ml −1 aqueous suspension stock. The lipid stock solution was flash-frozen in liquid nitrogen and stored at −80 °C. SDS–PAGE and immunoblotting SDS–PAGE was performed using homemade Tris-HCl 4-20% polyacrylamide gradient gels with Tris-glycine running buffer. Samples were mixed at a 1:1 ratio with 2× SDS sample loading buffer (100 mM Tris pH 6.8, 4% SDS, 20% glycerol, 0.05% bromophenol blue and 2% β-mercaptoethanol). SDS–PAGE gels were run for 45–60 min at 200 V. SDS–PAGE gels were stained with Coomassie Brilliant Blue (Alfa Aesar) and imaged using the ‘Gel’ feature of an Azure c400 imager (Azure Biosystems). For immunoblotting, proteins were transferred onto Immun-Blot PVDF membranes (Bio-Rad), incubated with sterile-filtered casein blocking buffer (Sigma Aldrich) for 1 h and then incubated with the appropriate antibodies. The following primary antibodies were used: anti-LPS core mouse monoclonal antibody (Hycult Biotechnology, HM6011, clone WN1 222-5, 1:5,000–1:20,000 dilution); anti-His-HRP (QIAGEN, 1:5,000 dilution); mouse anti-His HRP conjugate (BioLegend, 652504, 1:10,000 dilution); rabbit anti-LptD antiserum (provided by S. Matsuyama, 1:10,000 dilution); rabbit anti-LptA antiserum 21 ; rabbit anti-LptC antiserum 31 ; and rabbit anti-LptB antiserum 26 . The anti-LptA, anti-LptB and anti-LptC antisera were prepared by inoculating rabbits with purified protein prepared in the laboratory of D.K. The following secondary antibodies were used: donkey anti-rabbit HRP conjugate (GE Amersham, NA934-1ML, 1:10,000 dilution) and sheep anti-mouse HRP conjugate (GE Amersham, LNA931V/AH, 1:10,000 dilution). Bands were visualized using ECL Prime Western Blotting Detection Reagent (GE Amersham) and imaged using an Azure c400 (Azure Biosystems). Uncropped immunoblots are available in Supplementary Fig. 10 . Purification of LptB 2 FGCA for structural characterization C43(DE3) cells were transformed with pCDFDuetLptB 2 FG and pBAD-HisA-LptC-link-LptA-thr-His 7 . Overexpression and purification of the LptB 2 FGCA complexes were done similarly to the previously reported protocol for purification of LptB 2 FGC with some modifications 30 . Cultures were grown at 37 °C after diluting overnight cultures 1:100 into fresh LB broth supplemented with 50 μg ml −1 spectinomycin (Sigma) and 50 μg ml −1 carbenicillin (Teknova). Expression was induced with 300 μM isopropyl-β- d -1-thiogalactopyranoside (IPTG; Sigma) and 0.02% l -arabinose at an optical density at 600 nm (OD 600 nm ) of about 1, and cultures were grown for an additional 16–18 h at 18 °C. Cells were collected by centrifugation at 4,200 g for 20 min and resuspended in 20 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.0, 150 mM NaCl supplemented with 1 mM phenylmethanesulfonyl fluoride (PMSF, Sigma), 100 μg ml −1 lysozyme (Sigma) and 100 μg ml −1 DNase I (Sigma). Cells were passed through an EmulsiFlex-C5 high-pressure cell disruptor three times. Cell lysate was centrifuged at 10,000 g for 10 min to remove unbroken cells. Membranes were isolated by centrifugation at 100,000 g for 1 h. Membranes were resuspended and solubilized in 20 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.0, 150 mM NaCl, 10% glycerol and 1% n -dodecyl-β- d -maltopyranoside (DDM, Anatrace) at 4 °C for 2 h, followed by centrifugation at 100,000 g for 30 min. The supernatant was applied to Ni-NTA Superflow resin (QIAGEN) and the buffer was exchanged during the Ni-NTA purification to 20 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.0, 150 mM NaCl 10% glycerol, 0.01% DDM and 0.04% glycol-diosgenin (GDN). The protein was eluted with 20 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.0, 150 mM NaCl, 10% glycerol, 0.01% DDM, 0.04% GDN and 200 mM imidazole. The eluate was concentrated with an Amicon centrifugation filter with a 100-kDa molecular weight cut-off (MWCO; Amicon Ultra; Millipore), and subjected to SEC on a Superdex 200 increase 10/300 GL or a Superose 6 increase 10/300 GL column (GE Healthcare) in in 20 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.0, 150 mM NaCl, 1% glycerol, 1% dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO), 1% ethylene glycol and 0.02% GDN. Fractions were analysed by SDS–PAGE and selected fractions were used for the in vitro assembly of LptB 2 FGCADE in detergent (described below). For the structure of LptB 2 FGCA bound to LPS, the eluate after Ni-NTA affinity purification was incubated with a fivefold molar excess (final concentration approximately 160 μM) of LPS from E. coli EH100 dissolved in water (Ra mutant; Sigma) while sonicating for 15 min in ice water, and then incubated for a further 1 h on ice before purification by SEC. Fractions from SEC were pooled and concentrated to 7–8 mg ml −1 using a 100-kDa-MWCO Amicon filter and the protein was prepared for microscopy as described below. Purification of LptB 2 FGC(T47 p BPA)A was done as above with the following modifications. Protein was expressed from C43(DE3) cells transformed with pCDFDuetLptB 2 FG, pSup-BpaRS-6TRN and pBAD-HisA-LptC T47 p BPA -link-LptA-thr-His 7 . Cultures were grown at 37 °C after diluting overnight cultures 1:100 into fresh LB broth supplemented with 50 μg ml −1 spectinomycin (Sigma), 50 μg ml −1 carbenicillin (Teknova), 30 μg ml −1 chloramphenicol (Millipore Sigma) and 0.5 mM p BPA (Bachem). Expression was induced with 300 μM IPTG (Sigma) and 0.02% l -arabinose at OD 600 nm ≈ 0.6, and cultures were grown for an additional 3 h at 37 °C. Cells were collected by centrifugation at 4,200 g for 20 min and resuspended in 20 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.0 and 150 mM NaCl. To obtain LPS–LptC cross-links, the collected cells were resuspended in 500 ml of buffer consisting of 20 mM Tris pH 8.0 and 150 mM NaCl and exposed to UV light for 20 min on ice with mixing. Cells were collected by centrifugation at 4,200 g for 20 min and resuspended in 20 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.0, 150 mM NaCl and 2 mM MgCl 2 supplemented with 1 mM PMSF (Sigma), 100 μg ml −1 lysozyme (Sigma) and 100 μg ml −1 DNase I (Sigma) as above. The rest of the purification was performed as described for wild-type LptB 2 FGCA. Purification of LptB(E163Q) 2 FGCA was done as described above with the following modifications. Protein was expressed from C43(DE3) cells transformed with pCDFDuetLptB E163Q 2 FG and pBAD-HisA-LptC-link-LptA-thr-His 7 . During the membrane solubilization step, 2 mM ATP and 5 mM MgCl 2 were added to the solubilization buffer. The rest of the purification was performed as described for wild-type LptB 2 FGCA. Purification of LptD(Y63 p BPA)LptE for structural characterization C43(DE3) cells were transformed with pCOLADuet-LptE-His 6 -LptD Y63Am and pSup-BpaRS-6TRN plasmids. Overexpression and purification of the LptDE complexes was done similarly to the previously reported protocol for purification of LptDE with some modifications 22 . Cultures were grown at 37 °C after diluting overnight cultures 1:100 into fresh LB broth supplemented with 50 μg ml −1 kanamycin (Millipore Sigma), 30 μg ml −1 chloramphenicol (Millipore Sigma) and 0.5 mM p BPA (Bachem). Expression was induced with 500 μM IPTG (Sigma) at OD 600 nm ≈ 1, and cultures were grown for an additional 16–18 h at 26 °C. Cells were collected by centrifugation at 4,200 g for 20 min and resuspended in 20 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.0, 150 mM NaCl and 2 mM MgCl 2 supplemented with 1 mM PMSF (Sigma), 100 μg ml −1 lysozyme (Sigma), and 100 μg ml −1 DNase I (Sigma). Resuspended cells were passed through an EmulsiFlex-C5 high-pressure cell disruptor three times. The cell lysate was centrifuged at 10,000 g for 10 min to remove unbroken cells. Membranes were isolated by centrifugation at 100,000 g for 1 h. The membrane pellet was resuspended and solubilized in 20 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.0, 150 mM NaCl, 1.0% Anzergent 3-14 at 4 °C for 3 h and then ultracentrifuged as above. The supernatant was applied to Ni-NTA Superflow resin (QIAGEN) and the buffer was exchanged during the Ni-NTA purification first to 20 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.0, 150 mM NaCl 10% glycerol and 0.05% DDM and then to 20 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.0, 150 mM NaCl, 10% glycerol, 0.01% DDM and 0.04% GDN. The protein was eluted with 20 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.0, 150 mM NaCl, 10% glycerol, 0.01% DDM, 0.04% GDN and 200 mM imidazole. The eluate was concentrated with an Amicon centrifugation filter with a 100-kDa MWCO (Amicon Ultra; Millipore), and then subjected to SEC on a Superdex 200 increase 10/300 GL or a Superose 6 increase 10/300 GL column (GE Healthcare) in 20 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.0, 150 mM NaCl, 1% glycerol, 1% DMSO, 1% ethylene glycol and 0.02% GDN. Fractions were analysed by SDS–PAGE to assess the purification, and selected fractions were used for in vitro assembly of LptB 2 FGCADE in detergent. In vitro assembly of LptB 2 FGCADE complexes for structural characterization To assemble stabilized LptB 2 FGCADE complexes in detergent, approximately 2 mg of LptD(Y63 p BPA)E at a concentration of 1 mg ml −1 was mixed at a 1:1.1 molar ratio with approximately 3 mg of LptB 2 FGCA and incubated on ice for 15 min. The samples were exposed to UV light for 10 min on ice, mixing every 2 min. The cross-linked mixture was concentrated with an Amicon centrifugation filter, 100-kDa MWCO (Amicon Ultra; Millipore), and then subjected to SEC on a Superose 6 increase 10/300 GL column (GE Healthcare) in 20 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.0, 150 mM NaCl, 1% glycerol, 1% DMSO, 1% ethylene glycol and 0.02% GDN. Fractions were analysed by SDS–PAGE to assess the purification, and selected fractions were used for preparation of grids for cryo-electron microscopy. For preparation of the LPS-bound LptB 2 FGCADE complex (LPS-bound LptB 2 FGCADE; Fig. 1 and Extended Data Fig. 2 ), LptB 2 FGCA and LptD(Y63 p BPA)E were used. For preparation of the LptB 2 FGCADE complex without LPS (LPS-free LptB 2 FGCADE; Fig. 2 and Extended Data Fig. 4 ), LptB 2 FGC(T47 p BPA)A and LptD(Y63 p BPA)E were used. For preparation of the low-resolution LptB 2 FGCADE complex without LPS (Extended Data Fig. 5 ), LptB 2 FGCA and LptD(Y63 p BPA)E were used. For preparation of the ATP-bound LptB(E163Q) 2 FGCADE complex (ATP-bound LptB(E163Q) 2 FGCADE; Fig. 3 and Extended Data Fig. 8 ), LptB(E163Q) 2 FGCA and LptD(Y63 p BPA)E were used. Sample preparation for cryo-electron microscopy Proteins were purified as described above. All samples were prepared by plunge-freezing in liquid-nitrogen-cooled liquid ethane using a Thermo Fisher Scientific Vitrobot Mark IV. For the LPS-bound and LPS-free structures of LptB 2 FGCADE, purified protein (4 μl) was applied to glow-discharged C-flat 20 nm holey carbon 1.2-μm-hole-diameter, 1.3-μm-hole-spacing, 400-mesh copper grids (Protochips) and blotted for 7 s at 4 °C and 100% humidity with a wait time of 0, 15 or 30 s and the blot force set to 12. For the ATP-bound structure of LptB(E163Q) 2 FGCADE, purified protein was incubated on ice with 5 mM ATP and 5 mM MgCl 2 for 45 min with gentle agitation. For this sample, 0.65 mM fluorinated fos-choline-8 (Anatrace) was added immediately before plunge-freezing using the conditions described above. Sample (4 μl) was applied to glow-discharged C-flat 20 nm holey carbon 1.2-μm-hole-diameter, 1.3-μm-hole-spacing, 400-mesh copper grids (Protochips) and blotted for 6.5 s at 4 °C and 100% humidity with the blot force set to 12. Data acquisition For the LPS-bound and high-resolution LPS-free structures of LptB 2 FGCADE along with the LPS-bound structure of LptB 2 FGCA, image stacks were recorded using a Titan Krios G3i electron cryo-microscope (Thermo Fisher Scientific) operated at a 300-kV accelerating voltage. Image stacks (movies) were recorded on a Gatan BioQuantum K3 Imaging Filter (Gatan) using the super-resolution counting mode and a calibrated magnification of 105,000×, for a pixel size of 0.825 Å after 2× binning (for the LPS-free bridge structure) and 0.830 Å after 2× binning (for the LPS-bound LptB 2 FGCA structure), using SerialEM v.4.0.5 62 . For our LPS-bound LptB 2 FGCADE structure, movies were recorded using counted double-subtracted super-resolution mode with a pixel size of 0.415 Å. The slit of the energy filter was set to 20 eV with a defocus range between 1.1 and 2.2 μm. For the low-resolution structure of LPS-free LptB 2 FGCADE, image stacks were recorded using a Talos Artica electron cryo-microscope (Thermo Fisher Scientific) operated at 200 kV accelerating voltage. Image stacks (movies) were recorded on a Gatan BioQuantum K3 Imaging Filter (Gatan) using the super-resolution counting mode and a calibrated magnification of 36,000×, for a pixel size of 1.1 Å after 2× binning using SerialEM v.4.0.5 62 . The defocus range was between 1.2 and 2.6 μm. The subframe time was set to allow the collection of 50 subframes per image stack, with an electron dose rate of around 1–1.278 e − per Å 2 per frame. The total electron dose was 50–64 e − per Å 2 . The multi-shot scheme in SerialEM was used for data collection, with settings of nine holes per stage move and two shots per hole. For the ATP-bound structure of LptB(E163Q) 2 FGCADE, image stacks were recorded using a Titan Krios G3i electron cryo-microscope. Image stacks (movies) were recorded on a Falcon 4i direct electron detector with a Selectris energy filter (slit width 10 eV) using the super-resolution counting mode and a calibrated magnification of 165,000×, for a pixel size of 0.74 Å after 2× binning using EPU v.3.6. The slit of the energy filter was set to 10 eV with a defocus range between 1.1 and 3.0 μm. The electron dose rate was 0.6237 e − per Å 2 per frame. The total electron dose was 51.147 e − per Å 2 . Image processing and 3D reconstruction The movie frames were motion-corrected and dose-weighted and the contrast transfer function (CTF) parameters were estimated using CryoSPARC Live and the patch CTF estimation functionality in cryoSPARC 63 . For counted double-subtracted super-resolution images, micrographs were 2× binned during motion correction. For the LptB 2 FGCA structure, particle picking was done using the cryoSPARC blob picker. For LptB 2 FGCADE structures, particle picking was done using a self-trained Topaz model 64 . The model was trained iteratively using a combination of manual picks, picks selected by the previous best Topaz model and a curated set of particle picks that was generated using template-based picking. The templates used for the template-based picking were generated using manual picks, and the template-based picks used for Topaz training were curated by 2D and 3D classification followed by shift-based recentring. The best model had the expected number of particles per micrograph set to 150, although the training dataset ultimately had closer to 50 good particles per micrograph. The best model had the ResNet8 architecture, was trained with batch normalization turned off and trained without denoising the micrographs. In total, three custom models were used: one for the low-resolution LptB 2 FGCADE structure, one for the ATP-bound LptB 2 (E163Q)FGCADE structure and one shared for the LPS-free and LPS-bound LptB 2 FGCADE structures. Junk particles were filtered out by successive rounds of 2D classification in cryoSPARC. Initial models were generated using the ab initio reconstruction in cryoSPARC and particles were filtered by successive rounds of heterogeneous refinement. After an initial non-uniform refinement job, particles were subjected to local refinement. If applicable, the particle shifts calculated during local refinement were used to recentre the particles, the particles were re-extracted in a smaller box size to focus on only one half of the bridge and new initial models were generated using ab initio reconstruction. For the ATP-bound structure, the globally refined bridge was manually recentred to focus on the IM using cryoSPARC before particle re-extraction using a smaller IM-focused box size. Particles were further filtered by heterogenous refinement, after which they were subjected to non-uniform refinement, local CTF refinement, global CTF refinement (fit for beam tilt, beam trefoil and spherical aberration), local refinement with masks focusing on the relevant parts of the complex and reference-based motion correction. Note that, for the ATP-bound structure, 3D classification focused on LptB 2 was also used to generate initial volumes for heterogeneous classification. For all bridge structures, particle sets tools in cryoSPARC were used after focused classification before final map construction to ensure that all final maps came from the same particle sets. Masks were made either using the Segger tool in UCSF Chimera or using the molmap feature in UCSF Chimera 65 , 66 , 67 . For all structures, particle heterogeneity was analysed using both cryoDRGN and 3D variability analysis in cryoSPARC. Classification and/or masking in RELION and cryoDRGN did not yield improvements for any of our other structures 68 , 69 , 70 . Maps used for figures were filtered according to local resolution with B-factor sharpening in cryoSPARC; map sharpening using DeepEMhancer 71 was also tested without yielding improvements. Structural biology applications used in this project were compiled and configured by SBGrid 72 . Model building, refinement and validation Models were built using the relevant local refinements and then combined by rigidly fitting into the global map. The initial model of LptDE was generated using ModelAngelo 73 . The initial model of LptA was generated by docking in the crystal structure of LptA (Protein Data Bank (PDB) 2R1A ) 18 , and the initial model of the LptC periplasmic domain was generated using SwissModel 74 . LPS coordinates from the PDB (ligand code JSG ) were used to generate restraints for the ligand with the PRODRG server 75 . The published model of LPS-containing LptB 2 FG (PDB 6S8H ) 39 was used as the initial model for the IM portion of the LPS-containing bridge, and SwissModel was used to generate the initial model of LptB 2 FGC for the LPS-free bridge. The initial models were all docked into the relevant maps. The coordinates were then refined using PHENIX 76 , 77 . The model was further optimized using ISOLDE 78 accessed through ChimeraX 79 , 80 , 81 . Manual model building was done in Coot 82 . The LPS molecule in the LptB 2 FGCA structure was first manually fitted into the map and then real-space-refined in Coot. LPS atoms lacking clear density were manually deleted. The final models were visually inspected for general fit to the map, and further inspected using MolProbity, the residue-wise local quality estimation DAQ and CheckMySequence 83 , 84 , 85 . All residues in our models had DAQ Cα scores greater than 0, except for LptC residues 44–62 for the LptB 2 FGCADE–LPS structure (DAQ Cα > −0.5) and LptB residues 237–240 for the LPS-free LptB 2 FGCADE structure (DAQ Cα > −0.2). There were no reported errors by CheckMySequence. The model validation statistics are summarized in Extended Data Tables 1 and 2 . In the high-resolution LPS-free and LPS-bound structures of LptB 2 FGCADE, the periplasmic portions of LptFG (LptF residues 137–246, LptG residues 142–244 for the LPS-bound structure; LptF residues 139–243 and LptG residues 143–243 for the LPS-free structure) have low local resolution because of flexibility, and in the structure of LptB 2 FGCA the periplasmic portions of LptFGCA (LptF residues 146–236, LptG residues 150–236, LptC residues 38–183, all of LptA), also have low local resolution because of flexibility. For this reason, we did not build the model in these regions for PDB deposition. For visualization, the atomic models for the periplasmic portions of LptFG (LptF residues 146–236, LptG residues 150–236) in the two structures of LptB 2 FGCADE were generated by docking previously determined structures into our map (PDB 6MHU ) 38 without further refinement. For the low-resolution regions of LptB 2 FGCA (LptF residues 146–236, LptG residues 150–236, LptC residues 38–183, all of LptA), atomic models for visualization were generated by docking the relevant portion of the LPS-free LptB 2 FGCADE structure without further refinement. The low-resolution LPS-free structure of LptB 2 FGCADE is too low resolution for atomic model building. For visualization, we rigid-body-fitted the structures of LptB 2 FGC and LptDE generated using our high-resolution LPS-free dataset into the map without further refinement. Similarly, the ATP-bound structure of LptB 2 FGCADE is too low resolution for atomic model building. For visualization, we rigid-body-fitted PDB 6MI8 (a model corresponding to vanadate-bound LptB 2 FGC) and the structure of LptADE generated from our LPS-bound LptB 2 FGCADE dataset into the map without further refinement. We did not deposit a model for these two structures to the PDB because of these resolution constraints. Calculation of the internal volume of the periplasmic domains of the LPS-bound and LPS-free structures of LptB 2 FGCADE was done using pyKVFinder (v.0.9.2) accessed through ChimeraX (1.11.1) 37 , 79 , 80 , 81 . Purification of LptB 2 FG, LptB 2 FGC and LptB 2 FGCA complexes for reconstitution into proteoliposomes or detergent-based assays The LptB 2 FG, LptB 2 FGC and LptB 2 FGCA complexes used for reconstitution into proteoliposomes were purified as described for cryo-electron microscopy with the following modifications. The affinity buffer was 20 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.4, 150 mM NaCl, 15% glycerol and 0.05% DDM. The SEC buffer was 20 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.4, 150 mM NaCl, 5% glycerol and 0.05% DDM. After SEC, fractions were analysed by SDS–PAGE to assess the purification and selected fractions were pooled, concentrated to approximately 5 mg ml −1 , flash-frozen and stored at –80 °C until use. LptB 2 FG and LptB 2 FGC used for LPS release in detergent was purified as described for LptB 2 FGCA for cryo-electron microscopy with the following modifications. Carbenicillin (50 μg ml −1 ) was not added to the growth medium for expression of LptB 2 FG. Expression was induced with 200 μM IPTG. Expression of LptB 2 FG did not require the addition of 0.02% arabinose. The affinity buffer was 20 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.4, 300 mM NaCl, 15% (vol/vol) glycerol, 0.01% (wt/vol) DDM, and 0.04% (wt/vol) GDN. The SEC buffer was 20 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.4, 150 mM NaCl, 5% (vol/vol) glycerol and 0.02% GDN. After SEC, fractions were analysed by SDS–PAGE to assess the purification and selected fractions were pooled, concentrated to approximately 5 mg ml −1 , flash-frozen and stored at –80 °C until use. LptB 2 FGC(T47 p BPA)A(L116 p BPA) used for LPS release in detergent was purified as described for LptB 2 FGC(T47 p BPA)A for cryo-electron microscopy with the modifications listed above and the following. Protein was expressed from BL21(DE3) cells transformed with pCDFDuetLptB 2 FG, pSup-BpaRS-6TRN and pBAD-HisA-LptC T47 p BPA -thr-link-LptA L116 p BPA -His 7 . Cultures were grown with 0.8 mM p BPA. After induction, cultures were grown for 16–18 h at 18 °C before cells were collected. Collected cells were not exposed to UV light before protein purification. Purification of LptB(E163Q) 2 FG, LptB(E163Q) 2 FGC and LptB(E163Q) 2 FGCA complexes for SPA IM complexes used for SPA experiments were purified as described above with the following modifications. All complexes used for SPA had an E163Q mutation in LptB to trap the ATP-bound state. LptB(E163Q) 2 FG and LptB(E163Q) 2 FGC were expressed with an N-terminal His 6 tag on LptB to allow interaction with copper-coated PVT SPA beads (Perkin Elmer, Revvity). LptB(E163Q) 2 FGCA used to generate bridges was purified using a C-terminal His 7 tag on the LptCA fusion, as for structural samples. After Ni-NTA affinity purification, eluate was concentrated to approximately 5 mg ml −1 and split between the samples with and without LPS. The +LPS samples were incubated with a fivefold molar excess (final concentration approximately 160 μM) of LPS from E. coli EH100 dissolved in water (Ra mutant; Sigma) while sonicating for 15 min in ice water, and then incubated for a further 1 h on ice before purification by SEC. The −LPS samples were also purified by SEC. Cross-linked LptB(E163Q) 2 FGCADE bridges with or without LPS were prepared by incubating the prepared LptB(E163Q) 2 FGCA +LPS or −LPS samples with LptD(Y63 p BPA)E in the presence of UV light and purifying by SEC. For all samples, fractions were pooled after SEC, concentrated to approximately 5 mg ml −1 , flash-frozen and stored at –80 °C until use. Purification of the corresponding proteins from Acinetobacter baylyi was done as reported previously 58 , with the exception that the mutant that does not produce LPS 86 was used in place of the wild type and E. coli proteins were expressed instead of Acinetobacter ones. The amount of LPS bound to each sample was assessed by immunoblotting using an anti-LPS antibody (Hycult Biotechnology, HM6011, clone WN1 222-5, 1:5,000–1:20,000 dilution), with anti-LptB as a loading control 26 . Purification of LptDE for ATP hydrolysis and flow cytometry Overexpression and purification of LptDE wild-type and truncated complexes were done as previously reported 22 , 87 for the wild-type LptDE with minor modifications. In brief, an overnight culture containing C43(DE3) cells transformed with pCOLADuet-LptE-His 6 LptD was diluted 1:100 into 1.5-l flasks containing LB supplemented with 0.2% glucose and 30 µg ml −1 kanamycin. Cultures were grown at 37 °C until an OD 600 nm of around 0.6–0.8 and induced with 500 µM IPTG (Teknova) for 3–4 h at 37 °C. Cells were collected at 4,200 g for 10 min and resuspended in 20 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.0, 150 mM NaCl supplemented with a cOmplete protease tablet (Roche), 100 µg ml −1 lysozyme (Sigma) and 100 µg ml −1 DNase I (Sigma). The resuspended cells were passed through an EmulsiFlex-C3 high-pressure cell disruptor twice and centrifuged at 15,000 g for 20 min to remove unbroken cells. The supernatant was centrifuged at 100,000 g for 30 min to isolate membranes. The membranes were solubilized in 20 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.0, 150 mM NaCl and 0.5% n -lauroylsarcosine sodium salt (Sigma) supplemented with a cOmplete protease inhibitor tablet (Roche) at 4 °C for 2 h and centrifuged for 30 min at 100,000 g . The membrane pellet was resuspended in 20 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.0 and 150 mM NaCl and centrifuged for 30 min at 100,000 g to remove the remaining n -lauroylsarcosine sodium salt. The washed pellet was solubilized in 20 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.0, 300 mM NaCl, 20 mM imidazole and 1.0% Anzergent 3-14 (Anatrace) at 4 °C for 2 h and then centrifuged at 100,000 g for 1 h. The supernatant was applied to Ni-NTA Superflow (QIAGEN) and the flowthrough was collected and reapplied to the column. The column was washed with 20 column volumes of 20 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.0, 300 mM NaCl, 20 mM imidazole and 0.02% Anzergent 3-14 (Anatrace) followed by 20 column volumes of 20 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.0, 300 mM NaCl, 20 mM imidazole and 1.0% n -octylglucoside (OG, Anatrace). The column was eluted with six column volumes of 20 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.0, 300 mM NaCl, 200 mM imidazole and 1.0% OG (Anatrace). The eluate was concentrated with a 100-kDa-MWCO Amicon centrifugation filter and purified by SEC in 20 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.0, 150 mM NaCl and 1.0% OG. Fractions were pooled and concentrated with a 100-kDa Amicon centrifugation filter to approximately 5–10 mg m −1 . Purified complexes were analysed by SDS–PAGE. Samples were flash-frozen in liquid nitrogen and stored at −80 °C until use. Purification of LptA(I36 p BPA) LptA(I36 p BPA) was purified as described previously 23 . In brief, BL21(λDE3) E. coli cells containing pSup-BpaRS-6TRN and pET22b-LptA I36Am were grown to an OD 600 nm of about 0.5 at 37 °C in LB medium containing 50 μg ml −1 carbenicillin, 30 μg ml −1 chloramphenicol and 0.8 mM p BPA (Bachem). Cells were induced with 50 μM IPTG, allowed to grow for 2 h, collected, resuspended in a mixture containing 50 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.4, 250 mM sucrose and 3 mM EDTA, incubated on ice for 30 min and pelleted (6,000 g , 10 min). The supernatant was supplemented with 1 mM PMSF and 10 mM imidazole and pelleted (100,000 g , 30 min). The supernatant was incubated with Ni-NTA resin, which was washed twice (20 column volumes of 20 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.0, 150 mM NaCl, 10% glycerol and 20 mM imidazole). LptA was eluted with wash buffer supplemented with an additional 180 mM imidazole, concentrated using a 10-kDa-cut-off Amicon centrifugal concentrator (Millipore) to approximately 3 mg ml −1 , flash-frozen and stored at −80 °C until use. Purification of ΔTM-LptC To purify ΔTM-LptC, BL21 (λDE3) E. coli cells containing pBAD-HisA-LptC24-191-thrombin-His 7 were grown to an OD 600 nm of around 0.6 at 37 °C in LB medium containing 50 μg ml −1 carbenicillin. Cells were induced with 0.2% l -arabinose, allowed to overnight at 16 °C, collected and resuspended in lysis buffer (20 mM Tris pH 8.0, 150 mM NaCl and 10% glycerol). Lysozyme, DNase I and PMSF were added to final concentrations of 100 µg ml −1 , 50 µg ml −1 and 1 mM, respectively. Cells were passed through an EmulsiFlex-C3 high-pressure cell disruptor twice. The cell lysate was centrifuged (5,000 g , 10 min) and the supernatant was further centrifuged (100,000 g , 30 min). The supernatant was spiked with imidazole to a final concentration of 10 mM, and then rocked with Ni-NTA Superflow resin (QIAGEN) for 1 h. Protein was eluted with lysis buffer containing 200 mM imidazole, concentrated using a 10-kDa-MWCO Amicon Ultra centrifugal filter (Millipore) and purified by SEC on a Superdex 200 increase column in SEC buffer (20 mM Tris pH 8.0, 150 mM NaCl and 10% glycerol). Fractions were pooled and incubated with thrombin (BioVision) overnight at 4 °C. The solution was spiked with 8 mM imidazole and passed over a column containing Ni-NTA Superflow resin (QIAGEN) and Benzamidine Sepharose 4 Fast Flow resin (GE Healthcare) three times. The final flowthrough was concentrated, separated into 10-µl aliquots, flash-frozen and stored at −80 °C. Preparation of LptB 2 FG, LptB 2 FGC or LptB 2 FGCA-containing liposomes Proteoliposomes were prepared as described previously 23 . A mixture of 20 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.0, 150 mM NaCl, 7.5 mg ml −1 E. coli polar lipids, 0.5 mg ml −1 LPS and 0.25% DDM was prepared and kept on ice for 10 min. Purified LptB 2 FGC or LptB 2 FG was added to a final concentration of 0.86 μM, and the mixture was left on ice for 20 min. The mixture was diluted 100-fold with cold 20 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.0 and 150 mM NaCl and kept on ice for 20 min. The proteoliposomes were pelleted (300,000 g , 2 h, 4 °C), resuspended in 20 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.0 and 150 mM NaCl, diluted 100-fold and centrifuged (300,000 g , 2 h, 4 °C). The pellets were resuspended in a mixture of 20 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.0, 150 mM NaCl and 10% glycerol (250 μl per 100 μl of the original pre-dilution solution), homogenized by sonication, flash-frozen and stored at −80 °C until use. Preparation of LptDE-containing proteoliposomes Proteoliposomes containing LptDE-His 6 were prepared as previously reported 22 , 25 , with minor modifications as detailed here. A mixture of 20 mM Tris pH 8.0, 150 mM NaCl, 9 mg ml −1 lipid stock and 1.25% OG was prepared and kept on ice for 10 min. Purified LptDE was added to a final concentration of 1.43 µM and the mixture was incubated on ice for 10 min. The mixture was diluted 100-fold with cold 20 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.0 and 150 mM NaCl and kept on ice for 10 min. The proteoliposomes were pelleted (300,000 g , 2 h, 4 °C). The pellets were resuspended in a mixture of 20 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.0, 150 mM NaCl and 10% glycerol (22.5 μl per 100 μl of the original pre-dilution solution), homogenized by sonication, flash-frozen and stored at –80 °C until use. SPA to determine the ATP binding affinity of Lpt complexes ATP binding to LptB(E163Q) 2 FG, LptB(E163Q) 2 FGC, LptB(E163Q) 2 FGCA and LptB(E163Q) 2 FGCADE was assessed using an SPA adapted from a standard protocol 88 . Buffer conditions were adapted to match the structural studies of the Lpt complexes (20 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5, 150 mM NaCl, 3 mM MgCl 2 , 5% glycerol and 0.02% GDN). Lpt complex in detergent (50 nM) was incubated with ATP (4–600 μM total ATP), composed of a mixture of 0.2% [2,8- 3 H]-ATP (Perkin Elmer, Revvity) and 99.8% non-radioactive ATP (Sigma). Copper-chelated PVT SPA beads (Perkin Elmer) were added to a final concentration of 5 mg ml −1 . The mixture was dispensed in a clear-bottom, white 96-well plate (Corning 3604) and was mixed on a 96-well plate shaker (Eppendorf) at 900 rpm and 30 °C for 15 min, with 30 s shaking and 30 s resting. Signal to noise was optimal when SPA plates were kept 4 °C for about 36 h and shaken at 900 rpm as described, allowing beads to settle for 35 min before data collection. The SPA was performed at 25 °C in cpm mode (Perkin Elmer MicroBeta2). The total binding signal was background-corrected to account for non-proximity effects. Data are shown as mean ± s.d. from three experiments. Nucleotide binding was analysed by a specific binding model with cooperative slope using GraphPad Prism (see equation below, in which Y indicates binding, B max indicates maximum binding; h is the Hill coefficient; X denotes the ligand (ATP); and K d is the equilibrium dissociation constant). Raw data are in Supplementary Fig. 9 . $$Y=\frac{{B}_{\max }{[X]}^{h}}{{{K}_{{\rm{d}}}}^{h}+{[X]}^{h}}.$$ To visualize differences in K d in the overlaid datasets, the curve fit equations and raw data were all normalized to bind two ATP molecule equivalents (one per each subunit of LptB) at the calculated B max . This was done by dividing all data points for a curve by the calculated B max for the pertinent dataset and multiplying by two ATP equivalents. This treatment allows for simple visualization of all the curves as they converge towards a maximum of two ATP molecules bound, and does not alter the parameters of the Hill equation. ATPase assay using proteoliposomes ATPase assays were done using a modified molybdate method, as previously reported, with slight modifications 30 . ATPase reactions of proteoliposomes were performed in 20 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.0, 150 mM NaCl and 10% glycerol with varying concentrations of proteoliposomes. Proteoliposomes were mixed at varying ratios and allowed to incubate at 30 °C for 10 min to allow for bridge formation. Reactions were initiated at 30 °C by the addition of a pre-heated initiation buffer. The initiation buffer was added at 10% of reaction volume for a final concentration of 2 mM ATP and 2 mM MgCl 2 . Reactions were incubated at 30 °C, with aliquots taken at various time points. Aliquots were quenched with 12% sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS) at 1:1 vol/vol. ATPase experiments containing liposomes with LptB 2 FGCA and LptDE were run such that the LptB 2 FGCA concentration was 80 nM and LptDE was added to the stoichiometries indicated. The +LptDE reactions (Fig. 3g ) contained a final concentration of 4.48 μM of LptDE for a 56-fold excess, and reactions were done in triplicate. Titration data (Fig. 3f ) were collected in duplicate, except for the 64-fold excess of LptDE for the +LPS sample. The amounts of inorganic phosphate were determined using a colorimetric method as previously reported, with potassium phosphate used as a standard 89 . The absorbance at 850 nm (Spectramax 384 Plus) at each time point was measured 30 min after quenching in a transparent 384-well plate (Corning 3701). In vivo photocrosslinking In vivo photocrosslinking experiments were performed as previously described 23 , 30 with some modifications. The indicated strains were grown overnight in LB overnight at 37 °C supplemented with 0.2% glucose, 50 µg ml −1 spectinomycin, 50 µg ml −1 carbenicillin and 30 µg ml −1 chloramphenicol. Cultures were diluted 1:100 in fresh LB containing appropriate antibiotics and supplemented with 0.8 mM p BPA. Cultures were grown until an OD 600 nm of around 0.6, and then 0.02% arabinose and 200 µM IPTG were added. Cultures were grown for an additional 2 h, and then half of the culture was placed on ice and UV irradiated for 10 min. Cells were collected at 5,000 g for 10 min and pellets were resuspended in lysis buffer containing 20 mM Tris-HCl (pH 8.0), 300 mM NaCl supplemented with 1 mM PMSF, 50 µg ml −1 DNAse I, 100 µg ml −1 lysozyme and 5 mM MgCl 2 . Resuspended cells were freeze-thawed for three cycles and 1% Anzergent 3-14 was added to the lysate. All solubilized lysates were spun at 12,000 g for 10 min to remove insoluble debris. Clarified lysate was loaded onto 250 µl of Ni-NTA resin that had been washed with Milli-Q water and equilibrated with buffer containing 20 mM Tris-HCl, 300 mM NaCl and 0.1% Anzergent 3-14. Columns were washed with 20 column volumes of buffer containing 20 mM Tris-HCl, 300 mM NaCl, 0.1% Anzergent 3-14 and 20 mM imidazole. Columns were eluted with 750 µl followed by 600 µl of buffer containing 20 mM Tris-HCl, 300 mM NaCl, 0.1%, Anzergent 3-14 and 200 mM imidazole. All eluate samples were precipitated with 10% trichloroacetic acid and pellets were resuspended in 2× SDS–PAGE loading buffer normalized to the optical density of the original cultures. All samples were run on SDS–PAGE gels and immunoblotted with appropriate antibodies, as described above. LPS transport assay for LptB 2 FG and LptB 2 FGC in proteoliposomes The levels of release of LPS from proteoliposomes to LptA were measured as previously described 23 , 27 . Assays used 60% vol/vol proteoliposomes in a solution containing 50 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.0, 500 mM NaCl, 10% glycerol, 2 µM LptA(I36 p BPA) and 0.96 µM ΔTM-LptC where applicable. Reactions were initiated by the addition of ATP (varying concentration, as relevant) and 2 mM MgCl 2 , and proceeded at 30 °C. Samples were taken after 60 min, irradiated with UV light (365 nm) on ice for 10 min using a B-100AP lamp (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and analysed by SDS–PAGE and immunoblotting. Cross-linking of LPS to LptB 2 FGC(T47pBPA)A(L116 p BPA) in detergent LPS was diluted in buffer (20 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.0, 150 mM NaCl, 1.35 mM MgCl 2 , 10% glycerol and 0.02% GDN) to 34 μM. This mixture was sonicated for 30 s. Buffer (20 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.0, 150 mM NaCl, 10% glycerol and 0.02% GDN) and LptB 2 FGC(T47 p BPA)A(L116 p BPA) was added for a final concentration of 0.8 μM LptB 2 FGC(T47 p BPA)A(L116 p BPA) and 4 μM LPS. This mixture was incubated at 30 °C for 20 min. The reaction was initiated by the addition of 3 mM ATP and MgCl 2 . Samples were taken immediately after ATP addition, after 5 min, after 15 min and after 30 min. Immediately after collection, each sample was irradiated with UV light (365 nm) on ice for 10 min using a B-100AP lamp (Thermo Fisher Scientific), and 2× SDS–PAGE loading buffer was added to uncleaved samples immediately after UV irradiation. Thrombin-cleaved samples were treated with 1.5 units of thrombin (Cytiva) for 24 h at room temperature before 2× SDS–PAGE loading buffer was added. Samples were analysed by SDS–PAGE and immunoblotting as described above with the following modification: 10% Criterion Tris-HCl gels (Bio-Rad) were used to analyse uncleaved samples and 15% Criterion Tris-HCl gels (Bio-Rad) were used to analyse thrombin-cleaved samples. Ethics declarations The work did not involve human research participants. Harrison View author publications Search author on: PubMed Google Scholar Daniel Kahne View author publications Search author on: PubMed Google Scholar Contributions D.K. and R.J.T. conceived the project and designed research. R.J.T. designed and developed methods to stabilize and purify Lpt bridges. R.J.T. and K.S.P. performed cryo-EM experiments, with help from R.M.W. and A.C. K.S.P. designed the strategy to reconstruct Lpt structures from the cryo-EM data, and K.S.P. and R.J.T. solved and refined the structures with input from R.M.W. A.C. designed and performed ATP binding assays and S.J.R. designed and performed ATP hydrolysis experiments. V.B. designed and developed methods to obtain LPS-free Lpt. N.R. designed genetic experiments to validate the cellular functionality of the Lpt–LptA fusion, and performed them with S.A.E. and A.W. R.J.T. and S.J.R. confirmed bridge formation in vitro. S.A.E. designed and performed in vivo biochemical experiments in Fig. 4 , with supporting in vitro experiments performed by K.S.P. B.P. designed and performed in vitro experiments in Fig. 5 , with supporting in vivo experiments performed by S.A.E. D.K. and R.J.T. wrote the manuscript, with strategic input from S.C.H. R.J.T. and K.S.P. prepared the figures, with help from B.P., A.C., S.A.E. and S.J.R. All authors reviewed and edited the manuscript. Corresponding authors Correspondence to Rebecca J. Extended data figures and tables Extended Data Fig. 1 Design and validation of a LptC–LptA fusion protein to stabilize trans-envelope Lpt complexes. a , Cartoon of the IM complex containing the LptC–LptA fusion protein where LptC and LptA are connected by a poly-glycine-serine linker and comprise a single polypeptide. b , Locus analysis of ΔlptC , ΔlptA , and ΔlptCΔlptA strains by PCR. The expected sizes are 2,188 bp (wild type), 3,039 bp ( ΔlptC :: kan ), 3,057 bp ( ΔlptA :: kan ) and 2,513 bp ( ΔlptCA :: kan ). Four independent isolates of each strain were phenotypically characterized. After confirming that all selected isolates behaved the same phenotypically, one of them was kept after confirming the genotype by PCR. c , The LptC–LptA fusion plasmid complements ΔlptC , ΔlptA , and ΔlptCΔlptA strains. Spot dilutions were plated on M63 minimal medium. d , The quantities of LptC, LptA, and LptC–LptA present in lysate from ΔlptC , ΔlptA , and ΔlptCΔlptA strains complemented with the LptCA fusion were analysed by immunoblotting with anti-LptC and anti-LptA with anti-RpoA as a loading control. The blots shown are representative of 3 independent replicates. Blots against different antibodies represent identical samples processed in parallel. e , Site-specific in vivo photocrosslinking of LPS to LptC, LptA, or LptC–LptA. Proteins substituted at the indicated positions with the photocrosslinkable unnatural amino acid p BPA were overexpressed in E. coli . Samples were taken during mid-log phase, exposed to UV light and cross-linking was analysed by immunoblotting with anti-LPS with anti-His as a loading control. The blots shown are representative of 3 independent replicates. Blots against different antibodies represent identical samples processed in parallel. f , ATPase activity of LptB 2 FGC and LptB 2 FGCA in proteoliposomes with and without LPS. The data reported are the mean and standard deviation of three independent measurements. g , Flow cytometric analysis of Lpt bridge formation using fluorescently labelled proteoliposomes. IM proteoliposomes are labelled with ATTO-565 (y-axis, PE) and OM proteoliposomes are labelled with ATTO-488 (x-axis, FITC). Particles containing signal in both channels represent associated IM and OM proteoliposomes that have formed Lpt bridges. Protein combinations tested from left to right are: LptB 2 FGC + LptA + LptDE (positive control), LptB 2 FGCA + LptDE, and LptB 2 FGCA + truncated LptDE lacking the N-terminal periplasmic domain (negative control). h , Table summarizing the results of replicates from the flow cytometric analysis of Lpt bridge formation. The representative micrograph was chosen to contain approximately the median number of particles per micrograph out of particles included in the final reconstruction. d , Scheme of 3D classification and refinement of cryo-EM particle images. The resolution was determined at FSC = 0.143 (horizontal blue line). Extended Data Fig. 3 Volume of the periplasmic chute for LPS-bound and LPS-free Lpt bridges. a , Cartoon representation of the periplasmic domain of LPS-bound bridges is shown (left) together with a surface representation of the interior volume (centre). Constriction points where there is insufficient volume to accommodate the LPS substrate are indicated (right). b , Slices through the surface representations (coloured by hydrophobicity) of indicated regions of the periplasmic domain of LPS-bound bridges. c , Cartoon representation of the periplasmic domain of LPS-free bridges is shown (left) together with a surface representation of the interior volume (centre). Constriction points where there is insufficient volume to accommodate the LPS substrate are indicated (right). d , Slices through the surface representations (coloured by hydrophobicity) of indicated regions of the periplasmic domain of LPS-free bridges. The consensus map used for local refinement, low-pass filtered to 10 Å, is shown as a transparent outline. Subunits are coloured as follows: LptB, light brown; LptF, light green; LptG, light blue; LptC, pink; LptA, dark red; LptD, dark blue; LptE, orange. i , Two representations of the IM-focused local refinement of LptB 2 FGCADE. Bottom, IM-focused local refinement of LptB 2 FGCADE coloured by component as in h . Extended Data Fig. 7 Biochemical experiments relating to the role of the TM-LptC in LPS transport. a , LPS cross-linking to LptA(I36 p BPA) requires higher concentrations of ATP when the TM-LptC is present. Proteoliposomes containing purified IM complexes with or without the TM-LptC were tested for their ability to release LPS to LptA(I36 p BPA) with different concentrations of ATP added to the reaction. Samples were taken at 60 min, exposed to UV light and cross-linking was analysed by western blotting with anti-LPS with anti-LptA as a loading control. b , A mutation in the C-terminal β-strand of LptC (G153R) disrupts Lpt bridge formation. The position of the mutation (coloured yellow) is shown on the cartoon model of LPS-free LptB 2 FGCADE. Formation of LptB 2 FGCADE complexes was assessed by pulling down His-tagged wild-type or mutant variants of LptB 2 FGC and immunoblotting with antibodies against LptB, LptD, LptE and His-tag. c , Dissociation of the TM-LptC in vivo depends on assembly of Lpt bridges. Wild-type or mutant variants of LptB 2 FGC with p BPA incorporated at LptG I33 were photocrosslinked in vivo and adducts were detected by immunoblotting for antibodies against His-tag. The site where p BPA was incorporated (coloured yellow) is shown on the cartoon model of LPS-free LptB 2 FGCADE. d , Dissociation of the TM-LptC is required for LPS transport to LptC in vivo. Wild-type or mutant (G153R) variants of LptB 2 FGC with p BPA incorporated at LptC T47 and with or without the TM-LptC were photocrosslinked in vivo. LPS cross-linking was detected by immunoblotting with antibodies against LPS and His-tag. All western blot data presented in this figure is representative of 3 independent experiments. Blots against different antibodies represent identical samples processed in parallel. Extended Data Fig. 8 Cryo-EM data-processing workflow for LptB(E163Q) 2 FGCADE bound to ATP. a , SEC-FPLC trace of LptB(E163Q) 2 FGCAD(Y63 p BPA)E. The fractions that are highlighted in yellow were collected. b , SDS–PAGE gel showing the pooled peak fractions from the SEC-FPLC trace from a . c , Representative micrograph of LptB(E163Q) 2 FGCAD(Y63 p BPA)E. The representative micrograph was chosen to contain approximately the median number of particles per micrograph out of particles included in the final reconstruction. d , Representative 2D class averages of cryo-EM particle images focused on the full LptB(E163Q) 2 FGCAD(Y63 p BPA)E bridges. e , Representative 2D class averages of cryo-EM particle images focused on the IM portion of LptB(E163Q) 2 FGCAD(Y63 p BPA)E. f , Scheme of 3D classification and refinement of cryo-EM particle images. The initial models used for 3D classification were generated by ab initio reconstruction in cryoSPARC. The particle set used as the input for 3D variability analysis (Supplementary Fig. 4 and Supplementary Video 1 ) is indicated. g – j , Gold-standard Fourier shell correlation (FSC) curves calculated with different masks in cryoSPARC from the consensus map ( g ), locally refined structure of LptB 2 FGC ( h ), locally refined structure of LptADE ( i ) and higher-resolution locally refined structure of LptADE ( j ). The resolution was determined at FSC = 0.143 (horizontal blue line). Note that the higher-resolution structure of LptADE is from a larger particle set than the final local refinements for LptB 2 FGC and LptADE ( h , i ).
